GPS Triangle World Masters, Oschatz 2026

This is a coaching analysis of Bill Maisey's (Anglesey MAC) performance at the World Masters, Sport class, Oschatz 2026 - 38 pilots over 17 rounds, where Bill finished 22nd. It is built entirely from the public rcmodelspot GPS telemetry: every pilot's roughly 1 Hz track is recorded, so each round is compared like for like against the pilot who led Bill's own heat group and flew the same air, rather than against the overall winner in different conditions.

  • Performance Analysis

    Round by round against the same-air leader in each heat, decomposed by flight phase - cruise, climb, start and turns - and read against the day's conditions.

  • Recommendations

    The training actions that follow from the evidence, in priority order, with drills, further analysis, resources and rules-legal live-signal options.

  • Innovations

    The art of the possible for coaching technology, from a post-flight AI coach to a navigator heads-up display, each weighed against the Sport-class rules.

Performance Analysis

Bill flew a clean, consistent World Masters and finished mid-field. The data points to one dominant lever and a clear order behind it: this overview sets out the headline, then scoring and pace, start energy, and the conditions, trajectory and climbing that separate skill from air. Every figure is drawn from his own flights against the same-air leader each round.

  • 22nd of 38 (12,562 pts); the gap is almost all distance-task
  • Cruise speed between thermals is the dominant lever
  • Start is already competitive; the winner flies Bill's airframe
  • Stronger in strong lift; wider circles and more time off the course line

The Overall Read. Across all 17 rounds Bill (green) sits below his same-air round winner (blue) on score, laps and cruise speed, while matching everyone at the start gate. The gap tracks the day's lift, and event winner Florian Griese (grey) marks the benchmark - though from his own group, not Bill's air.

Within-Group Rank. Judged fairly against his own same-air group each round, Bill lands mid-pack; his best relative rounds line up with the strongest lift.

Gap Breakdown. Where the 2,887-point gap comes from, each pilot's worst round dropped: about 76% is the distance task and 24% the one-lap speed sprint, while landings and penalties add nothing.

Where The Ground Is Lost. Bill's clean lap is about 22 s slower than his same-air leader's. 90% of that is the straight glide between thermals; only 10% is turns and lines. In cost order the levers are cruise speed, then climb quality, then entry speed, then turns - cruise pace dominates.

What to do. Train fastest-first: cruise pace between thermals (the ~2.7-lap pace effect), then climb quality for weak-lift days, then a cheap win by using the entry-speed cap; turns and lines are the smallest lever. He matched the leader lap-for-lap in Rounds 7 and 17, so the ceiling is there. The 120 km/h entry cap and scoring are set in the Sport-class regulations; field data from the event results.

Consistency: Floor Vs Ceiling. The score is dragged down by a few weak-lift rounds, not by the good ones falling short. The two bombouts (R12 = 418, dropped; R9 = 581) sit far below the median of 794.

The Ceiling Holds. Round 17: Bill (green) tracks the same-air leader Jens Geider (teal) lap-for-lap to a near-perfect 999. When lift is good the top-end pace is already there.

What to do. A bombout costs more than a strong round gains, so the fastest ranking win is raising the floor - staying aloft through weak, scratchy lift - rather than chasing the ceiling. This is the weak-lift climb work again, seen from the results side. Round scores: event results (rcmodelspot).

Progression Across The Week. Splitting conditions from skill, there is no clear week-long practice trend. Both series swing round to round with the air; his two strongest normalised results (Rounds 7 and 17) are a first-day and a last-day flight, not the ends of a rising line.

What to do. Round-to-round conditions dominate the record far more than any drift in form, so read single rounds cautiously and judge progress on the conditions-controlled score, not on laps. With n ≈ 14 the trend signal is weak either way. Per-round scores: event results (rcmodelspot).

Landings: A Clean Sweep. Bill scored the full 600 landing points on every one of the 14 distance rounds and drew no zone or airspace penalties all week - the clean-execution baseline the lap-count work builds on.

Scoring, Laps & Speed

Collapseback to top

Score Per Round. Every round's normalised score - his same-air round winner (blue), event winner Florian Griese (grey) and Bill (green). Bill trails the round-winning pace in most distance rounds, and Griese is not always top of his own group either.

Laps Per Round. Laps decide the distance score, and Bill's bars sit below the round winner almost everywhere - the gap widening on weak-lift days. The winner's blank at Round 9 is his own bombout.

Cruise Speed. Pace drives laps, and Bill's average task speed runs consistently below the round winner's - the dominant lever behind the laps gap.

Field Position & The Laps/Speed Scatter. Every pilot's average task speed against average laps over the 14 distance rounds; Bill (green) sits low-left - fewer laps because the average pace is slower. Laps decide the score, and pace drives laps.

Speed Gaps. Clean-lap cruise 61.9 vs 67.4 km/h (~8% slower). At the start gate Bill crosses at 71 vs 95 km/h, leaving ~49 km/h of the 120 km/h cap unused - free opening-lap energy.

What to do. Laps decide the score and pace drives laps, so the dominant training lever is cruise pace between thermals, with climb quality closing the weak-lift days. Round winner is Bill's same-air group leader (fair, same-conditions); the event winner flew a different group, so his absolute laps and speed reflect his own air. Per-round scores and laps: event results (rcmodelspot).

Start Energy

Collapseback to top

Entry Speed. Bill routinely crosses the start gate slower than the round winner, leaving free opening-lap energy on the table. Only Bill and each round's same-air winner were track-analysed, so the event winner is absent here.

Entry Altitude. Bill and the round winner both start near the ceiling, so entry altitude is not a lever. Event winner omitted for the same telemetry reason as entry speed.

What to do. Entry height is already maxed, so the free win at the gate is crossing nearer the 120 km/h speed cap. The 120 km/h entry cap and the wing-loading limits below are set in the Sport-class regulations.

The Airframe Question. The top of the Sport-class field is an airframe mix, not a monoculture, and event winner Florian Griese flies the Pike Paradigm (Samba Model) - the same airframe Bill flies - so the ~2,900-point gap between them is a technique and task-execution gap, not an equipment one. The class rules reinforce this: every Sport-class glider is capped at 5 m span, 7 kg all-up weight and 75 g/dm2 wing loading, compressing the envelope so no legal airframe holds a decisive edge (Sport-class regulations). As general aerodynamics rather than a measured difference in this field, a cleaner or more heavily ballasted airframe can carry more speed and hold a flatter glide (higher L/D) while lighter wing loading tightens the turn for weak lift - trade-offs a pilot dials in with ballast and flap presets, not gains fixed in the kit. Published glide-ratio figures for these specific models were not found, so treat the aerodynamic points as directional, not measured.

Conditions, Trajectory & Climbing

Collapseback to top

Conditions Dependence. Wind shows no association with Bill's relative standing, but thermal strength does: his within-group score tends to rise with stronger lift - a moderate positive correlation (Spearman ρ ≈ +0.6, with laps following at about +0.5). His weakest relative rounds cluster in weak, late-day lift.

What to do. He is competitive when lift is strong and slips when it is scarce, which points the same way as climb quality: weak-lift persistence is the condition-specific fix. Read this as suggestive only - n ≈ 14 distance rounds, not a significance claim. Weather from Open-Meteo ERA5, flights from the event results.

Trajectory Trends. Most flight time is spent lapping right on the course line, so the frequency axis is logarithmic to expose the rare far excursions. The best pilots are bimodal - tightest to the course most of the time, yet happy to range much further and for longer when chasing lift. Bill sits in a moderate mid-band (median 46.8 vs the winner's 37.0 m).

Thermal Strength & Weather. The usable thermal-strength proxy. Read the laps against this strip: Bill's gap to the round winner grows as the lift pales.

Climb Geometry. Bill banks 41 m per thermal against the leader's 63 m (~35% less), in wider circles (39 vs 33 m radius). Yet he spends less total time circling (287 vs 402 s) - he is not over-thermalling; weak climbs make him land early on poor-lift days.

Climb Rate. The same climb-quality gap in vertical speed: Bill climbs at 0.89/2.55 vs the leader's 1.03/3.64 m/s (mean/best).

Thermalling Turn Radius. Inside sustained climbs Bill circles about 30% wider than the winner (median 38.0 vs 29.2 m). Wider circles sink more of each turn into repositioning than climbing - the same climb-quality lever, seen in the turn itself.

Round 12: A Worked Example. One round makes the pooled patterns concrete: the leader breaks well off the course line to work better lift and circles tighter, while Bill holds a neater but slower line - the off-course ranging and tighter turns the density charts summarise, in a single flight.

Round 1 - 3 Aug 12:55

Round 1 (3 Aug 12:55, Heat 1) is a distance task. Bill completed 7 laps to the same-air leader Ralph Losemann's 10 (3 short), scoring 751 of a possible 1000. The benchmark is the top scorer in his own heat - same time slot, same air. Full standings on the event results.

Visual Overview of Performance

Collapseback to top

Bill completed 7 laps to Ralph Losemann's 10 - 3 short - for 751 of a possible 1000 and 8th of 9 in the group. The gap was cruise pace: 24.9 km/h to Ralph Losemann's 34.1 (9.2 km/h slower), a deficit that compounds over the window into the 3-lap shortfall. Lift was strong, with 6 km/h wind. He also left energy at the gate, crossing at 75.1 km/h to Ralph Losemann's 101.4 and well under the 120 km/h cap. The steepest divergence came at 9:31-10:31: Leader gained 2 lap(s) here while Bill held station (slow lap / weak line). Figures reconcile to the event results.

Energy Management

Collapseback to top

Bill flew lower than Ralph Losemann for essentially the whole flight, averaging about 51 m down early and 168 m down late - and the gap widened. Across the task he banked about 1075 m of climb to the leader's 1253 m, working off a low near 148 m, while his speed trace runs below the leader's between thermals. Less height in hand forces earlier, slower glides, and the lap count follows.

Ground Track & Course

Collapseback to top

Bill's racing line was about as efficient as Ralph Losemann's (line ratio 1.01), so the ground track was not where this round was lost. His turn circles ran wider too, averaging 39 m to Ralph Losemann's 35 m. Turnpoint technique is near a strength; the loops, not the corners, are where the height - and the time - go, so wider, slower circles cost most.

Cumulative Laps vs Leader

Collapseback to top

Bill kept pace with Ralph Losemann through the first half, then fell away in the back half where most of the 3-lap gap opened. He held 24.9 km/h to the leader's 34.1 while that step line pulled clear to 10 laps. A slower average lap - mostly slower cruise between thermals - is what compounds into the shortfall.

Biggest-Loss Segment

Collapseback to top

Single biggest-loss window: 9:31-10:31 (60 s). Leader gained 2 lap(s) here while Bill held station (slow lap / weak line).

This is the steepest part of the divergence on the cumulative-laps and Energy Management charts above: one weak segment where the leader banked a clean lap and Bill did not. Recovering even half of these windows across the week is worth roughly a lap a round. Source: event results.

What to Train from This Round

Collapseback to top

The gap here is cruise pace between thermals - the biggest lever overall. Focus on faster inter-thermal cruise, with free opening-lap energy available from a fuller entry speed.

Visual Overview of Performance

Collapseback to top

Round 4 is the one-lap speed dash - a separate flat-out task scored across all 38 pilots, not the group's endurance race. Bill clocked 109.1 km/h on the single lap to run leader Ralph Losemann's 156.4 km/h - a 47.3 km/h shortfall for 29th of 38 and 695 points. He crossed the start about 46 m under the 400 m ceiling while Ralph Losemann banked nearly the full height (399 m), so the leader had more stored energy to trade for speed. With no lift to work, the whole gap is top-end cruise and a full-energy entry - the same speed lever as the distance rounds, isolated to one run. Figures reconcile to the event results.

Energy Management

Collapseback to top

Off much the same start height, Bill turned less of it into pace than Ralph Losemann - 109.1 km/h to 156.4 km/h over the single lap. Both traces bleed altitude for speed through the lap, but his ground-speed line sits below the leader's from the first straight. A cleaner high-energy entry and a faster glide line would convert the same height into more lap speed - the cruise lever isolated to one run.

Ground Track & Course

Collapseback to top

With no lift to hunt, both lines stay pinned to the course, so the sprint turns on how much speed each carried through the corners. His turn circles ran wider too, averaging 216 m to Ralph Losemann's 90 m. Tighter corners and a straighter run between turnpoints are the only time on offer - it comes down to carried speed.

Single-Lap Speed Task

Collapseback to top

There is no lap count to build on the sprint - the result is one flat-out lap, and Bill's ran 109.1 km/h to Ralph Losemann's 156.4 km/h. That was worth 695 points and 29th of 38 on the event results. The reward is raw pace and a full-energy entry, not endurance, so the lever is top-end cruise speed rather than lasting the distance.

Recommendations

The recommendations that follow from the analysis, grouped by implementation theme and ordered by how much each would move Bill's score. Each theme links back to the evidence that motivates it and, where relevant, out to the matching Innovations tier.

  • Train faster inter-thermal cruise (top lever)
  • Bank more height per climb on weak days
  • Use more of the entry-speed cap
  • Tighten turnpoint lines (near a strength)
  • Audio vario and speech telemetry callouts, today

Cruise Speed Between Thermals

Collapseback to top

Cruise pace between thermals is the single biggest lever. On clean laps Bill glides at 61.9 km/h against the same-air leader's 67.4 km/h, roughly 8% slower, at a shallower glide ratio (9.3 vs 10.3). That gap is about 90% of his 22 s per-lap clean-lap deficit, and a pace counterfactual attributes about +2.7 of the roughly three-lap shortfall to speed alone. Laps decide the score, so cruise pace is the underlying cause of the lower lap count (see the ranked phase levers in Analysis).

Drills

  • Speed-to-fly discipline: hold a higher glide speed between climbs and resist the instinct to stretch every glide flat.
  • Fly to a target inter-thermal cruise speed for the day's conditions rather than a habitual comfortable pace.
  • Cut altitude spent loitering at low value - convert height into distance while the air is sinking anyway.

Further Analysis

  • Per-leg speed against wind direction once a task file with turnpoint coordinates is available, to separate true cruise pace from head/tail-wind legs.

Climb Quality - Height Banked Per Thermal

Collapseback to top

Climb quality is the second lever, and it decides the weak days. Bill actually circles less than the leader in total (287 vs 402 s), so he is not over-thermalling; but he banks about 35% less height per thermal (40.7 vs 63.1 m) with wider, slower circles (39.4 vs 33.2 m radius; 0.89/2.55 vs 1.03/3.64 m/s mean/best climb). When lift is scarce this makes him land early - three laps in R9, two in R12 - which is where the lap-count shortfall opens up (phase levers; floor-vs-ceiling consistency).

Drills

  • Tighter, better-centred circles: work the core rather than orbiting it.
  • Bank-angle discipline - a consistent, committed bank to shrink the turn radius toward the leader's 33 m.
  • Commit to weak cores instead of leaving to search; patience before abandoning lift on poor-lift days.

Further Analysis

  • Per-thermal centring traces (drift-corrected) to quantify how much of the height gap is radius versus core selection.

Where Technology Could Help

A better real-time picture of climb rate and where the core sits is exactly what the navigator AR HUD and live AI cueing tiers target.

Entry Speed - Use the 120 km/h Cap

Collapseback to top

Entry speed is a cheap early win. Bill crosses the start gate at 70.8 km/h against the leader's 94.5 km/h, leaving about 49 km/h of the 120 km/h cap unused - roughly twice the leader's unused margin. His entry altitude is already at the cap, so this is free opening-lap energy left on the table (see the entry-speed lever).

Drills

  • Build and carry start-gate speed up toward the 120 km/h cap on the run-in, so the first lap starts with the energy the rules allow.
  • Practise the timed dive-to-gate so the peak speed lands on the line, not before or after it.

Turnpoint Lines

Collapseback to top

Turnpoint lines are already close to a strength - treat this as fine-tuning. Bill's lines run about 15 m per lap wider than the leader's, and turn technique costs only around 2 s per lap (about 10% of the deficit), the smallest of the four levers (phase levers, ranked).

Drills

  • Modest line tightening at the turnpoints, without bleeding the speed that the cruise lever is there to build - the two must not fight.

Rules-Legal Live Signals

Collapseback to top

Several live aids are legal today and need no new rules. A pilot may field one navigator whose role includes relaying telemetry, and both an audio vario and spoken telemetry callouts are explicitly permitted. None of these feed data into control of the model, so they stay inside the Sport-class rules (the same permitted channel the live-cueing tier builds on).

Set up now

  • Audio vario tuning: shape the tone gradient tightly around the core so small changes in climb rate are audible, not just present or absent.
  • Speech telemetry callouts through the radio - climb rate, altitude band, distance-to-turn - so Bill keeps his eyes on the model.
  • A navigator working the ground station, calling the telemetry picture and the tactical decision points.

Resources

  • SM-Modellbau GPS-Logger 3 - logger with audio vario and speech telemetry output.
  • OLC-RC (Online Contest) - track upload and comparison for structured post-session review.
  • BMFA Silent Flight Technical Committee - GPS - the discipline's rules and equipment guidance.

Future extensions

These same permitted channels are the foundation the navigator AR HUD, live AI cueing and post-flight AI coach tiers extend.

Innovations

The art of the possible for coaching technology, ordered from the most tractable to the most ambitious. Each tier is framed against the Sport-class rules (regulations): passive telemetry display and relay are permitted and a navigator may relay them, but nothing may feed data into control of the model (section 2.7). Where a tier touches competition rather than training, the legality consideration is stated plainly.

  • Post-flight AI coach on this same data (most tractable)
  • Navigator AR HUD (organiser discretion)
  • Live cueing within the rules
  • A season-long data flywheel

Post-Flight AI Coach

Collapseback to top

A post-flight AI coach is the most tractable step, and this report is the proof of concept. The same pipeline that built this analysis can be pointed at any event or flight - straight from the open rcmodelspot data, or from an IGC log - to generate the round-by-round, phase-by-phase read automatically. On top of that it can drive a ghost replay of Bill against the same-air leader and flag recurring decision points, such as the glides where he consistently gives back cruise time or the climbs he leaves early.

Legality Consideration. No competition constraint: this is offline analysis of flights already flown, so it sits entirely in the training and debrief space. Track upload and comparison already exist through OLC-RC.

Navigator AR HUD

Collapseback to top

A navigator AR HUD re-presents telemetry that is already permitted, in a form that is faster to read. Climb rate, energy state, distance-to-turn, line deviation and a live thermal map could sit in the navigator's field of view instead of being read off a screen and spoken. Hardware matters here: today's Ray-Ban Meta glasses are audio and camera only with no display, so a visual HUD needs display-class glasses (for example Ray-Ban Display) or AR glasses such as Xreal or Rokid.

Legality Consideration. The regulations do not name AR or wearables. A navigator-worn HUD that only re-presents permitted passive telemetry - feeding nothing into control of the model - is plausibly legal at Contest-Director discretion; a pilot-worn HUD is safest treated as training-only until organisers rule on it (Sport-class regulations).

Live AI Cueing

Collapseback to top

Live AI cueing turns the permitted speech channel into tactical calls. Telemetry streamed to a real-time engine could produce spoken prompts - commit to this core, push the glide, turn now - relayed by the navigator, plus a structured debrief the moment the flight lands. It is the natural extension of the audio vario and speech callouts that are already worth setting up today.

Legality Consideration. Spoken telemetry and an audio vario are explicitly permitted, and a navigator may relay them, so the audio path is legal in competition provided the cue is passive relay and nothing feeds into control of the model (regs section 2.7). The post-session debrief is unconstrained training use.

The Data Flywheel

Collapseback to top

A data flywheel compounds every flight into sharper coaching. Accumulating Bill's tracks together with the wider field's would support counterfactual what-if-you-had-stayed simulation on the climbs he left early, condition playbooks that map the day's weather to a tactical plan, and opponent profiling of how the strongest pilots handle weak lift. Each event ingested makes the next read better - the post-flight coach is the first turn of this wheel.

Legality Consideration. Purely offline and historical: no in-flight component, so no competition constraint. It depends only on the open track data already published per event.
